In mathematics, '''concavification''' is the process of converting a non-concave function to a [[concave function]]. A related concept is '''convexification''' – converting a non-convex function to a [[convex function]]. It is especially important in [[economics]] and [[mathematical optimization]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Li|first1=D.|last2=Sun|first2=X. L.|last3=Biswal|first3=M. P.|last4=Gao|first4=F.|date=2001-07-01|title=Convexification, Concavification and Monotonization in Global Optimization|journal=Annals of Operations Research|language=en|volume=105|issue=1–4|pages=213–226|doi=10.1023/A:1013313901854|s2cid=7570136 |issn=0254-5330}}</ref>

== Concavification of a quasiconcave function by monotone transformation ==
An important special case of concavification is where the original function is a [[quasiconcave function]]. It is known that:
* Every concave function is quasiconcave, but the opposite is not true.
* Every [[Monotonic function|monotone]] transformation of a quasiconcave function is also quasiconcave. For example, if <math>f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}</math> is quasiconcave and <math>g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}</math> is a monotonically-increasing function, then <math>x \mapsto g(f(x))</math> is also quasiconcave.
Therefore, a natural question is: ''given a quasiconcave function'' <math>f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}</math>, ''does there exist a monotonically increasing'' <math>g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}</math> ''such that'' <math>x \mapsto g(f(x))</math> ''is concave?'' 

=== Example and Counter Example ===
As an example, consider the function <math>x \mapsto f(x) = x^2</math> on the domain <math>x\geq 0</math>. This function is quasiconcave, but it is not concave (in fact, it is strictly convex). It can be concavified, for example, using the monotone transformation <math>t \mapsto g(t) = t^{1/4}</math>, since <math>x \mapsto g(f(x))=\sqrt{x}</math> is concave.

Not every concave function can be concavified in this way. A counter example was shown by Fenchel.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Convex cones, sets and functions|last=Fenchel|publisher=Princeton University|year=1953}}</ref> His example is: <math>(x,y) \mapsto f(x,y) := y + \sqrt{x+y^2}</math>. Fenchel proved that this function is quasiconcave, but there is no monotone transformation <math>g : \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> such that <math>(x, y) \mapsto g(f(x,y))</math> is concave.<ref name="Connell 2012" />{{Rp|7–9}}

Based on these examples, we define a function to be '''concavifiable''' if there exists a monotone transformation that makes it concave. The question now becomes: ''what quasiconcave functions are concavifiable?''

=== Concavifiability ===
Yakar Kannai treats the question in depth in the context of [[utility function]]s, giving sufficient conditions under which continuous [[convex preferences]] can be represented by concave utility functions.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1977-03-01|title=Concavifiability and constructions of concave utility functions|journal=Journal of Mathematical Economics|language=en|volume=4|issue=1|pages=1–56|doi=10.1016/0304-4068(77)90015-5|issn=0304-4068|last1=Kannai|first1=Yakar}}</ref>

His results were later generalized by Connell and Rasmussen,<ref name="Connell 2012">{{Cite journal|last1=Connell|first1=Christopher|last2=Rasmusen|first2=Eric Bennett|date=December 2017|title=Concavifying the QuasiConcave|journal=Journal of Convex Analysis|language=en|volume=24|issue=4|pages=1239–1262}}</ref> who give necessary and sufficient conditions for concavifiability. They show that the function <math>(x,y) \mapsto f(x,y) = e^{e^x}\cdot y</math> violates their conditions and thus is not concavifiable. They prove that this function is strictly quasiconcave and its gradient is non-vanishing, but it is not concavifiable.
